name: Cognitive Load
claim: Total mental effort is intrinsic plus extraneous plus germane; only the extraneous term is yours to cut, and cutting it frees capacity.
key_number: ~4 chunks capacity (Cowan 2001); 3 load types (Sweller 1994)
formula: Intrinsic + Extraneous + Germane <= working memory capacity
design_lever: Name the user segment, name which load term you are cutting, and predict one observable: error rate on field N, time-to-first-action, or abandonment at step 3.
anti_pattern: Do not argue reduce cognitive load in the abstract. A load claim with no named segment and no predicted metric is an aesthetic preference wearing a lab coat.
symptoms: this screen feels overwhelming|too much on one page|users miss details here|people give up halfway|it looks cluttered
quote: The amount of mental resources needed to understand and interact with an interface. - lawsofux.com

name: Miller's Law
claim: Immediate memory holds about 7 plus or minus 2 chunks rather than bits, and the modern controlled estimate is nearer 4.
key_number: 7+-2 chunks (Miller 1956); 4+-1 (Cowan 2010)
design_lever: Plan for 4 items maximum that a user must carry unaided across a screen boundary, and chunk every numeric sequence in the input field, not only in the display.
anti_pattern: Never cap a visible list at seven. Nesting a 40-item settings list into five menus of seven converts a cheap visual scan into an expensive chain of recalled decisions.
symptoms: how many items should this menu have|is seven too many tabs|users forget what they picked on the previous step|should we split this list
quote: Don't use the 'magical number seven' to justify unnecessary design limitations. - lawsofux.com

name: Working Memory
claim: The user's buffer holds 4 to 7 chunks for 20 to 30 seconds without rehearsal, and whatever it holds is capacity unavailable for thinking.
key_number: 4-7 chunks, 20-30 s without rehearsal; Brown-Peterson ~18 s
design_lever: Externalise every piece of state the system already knows: style visited links, keep breadcrumbs, show a comparison table instead of sequential pages, and never clear a form on validation error.
anti_pattern: Do not fire a modal in the middle of a comparison. An interruption does not delay the buffer, it flushes it, and the user restarts the task from the beginning.
symptoms: users keep flipping between two screens|they have to re-enter everything after an error|people lose their place|the wizard forgets what I typed
quote: Place burden of memory on the system, not the user. - lawsofux.com

name: Chunking
claim: Grouping items into meaningful units multiplies effective capacity, because the buffer counts units and units can be made arbitrarily large.
key_number: effective items ~ 4 x items_per_chunk
design_lever: Group with whitespace first and reach for borders only when proximity cannot carry it, and label each group with a word the user would use rather than the team's word.
anti_pattern: Do not group by internal taxonomy. Settings grouped by which team owns them are visually perfect and cognitively useless, and design review cannot catch it because the reviewer shares the model.
symptoms: this page is a wall of text|users cannot find the setting|the form feels endless|the nav has thirty items
quote: A process by which individual pieces of an information set are broken down and then grouped together in a meaningful whole. - lawsofux.com

name: Selective Attention
claim: Users filter to goal-relevant stimuli, so prominence and attention are not monotonically related and more emphasis can produce less attention.
key_number: none; selection depth scales with perceptual load
design_lever: Before enlarging anything, check four things in order: is it in an ad-shaped slot, does it resemble an ad, is another change firing at the same moment, is the user task-loaded.
anti_pattern: Do not answer users are not seeing X by making X bigger and redder. If X is being filtered rather than missed, extra prominence strengthens the ad resemblance and makes it worse.
symptoms: nobody notices the banner|users miss the error message|they swear the button was not there|the notice in the right rail gets ignored
quote: Users have learned to ignore content that resembles ads, is close to ads, or appears in locations traditionally dedicated to ads. - lawsofux.com

name: Serial Position Effect
claim: In a temporally presented sequence the first and last items are recalled best and the middle is lost.
key_number: recency dies after a ~30 s filled delay (Glanzer & Cunitz 1966)
design_lever: Put the cheap items in the middle of any sequence - onboarding steps, tutorial content, list order - and reserve the two ends for what the user must retain afterwards.
anti_pattern: Do not win a navigation-layout argument with a memory claim. A horizontal bar is visible at recall time; scan pattern and pointer economics predict the same layout without invoking memory.
symptoms: what order should the nav items go in|users forget the middle steps|where should the primary action sit|which plan should be listed first
quote: Users have a propensity to best remember the first and last items in a series. - lawsofux.com

name: Fitts's Law
claim: Time to acquire a target grows with distance and shrinks with target size, logarithmically in the ratio of the two.
key_number: 44 pt iOS / 48 dp Android / 24 px WCAG 2.2 SC 2.5.8
formula: MT = a + b*log2(2A/W); Shannon form MT = a + b*log2(A/W + 1)
design_lever: Get every control above the platform minimum, then stop optimising size and start cutting travel distance from wherever the eye and the pointer already are.
anti_pattern: Do not make the hit area equal the visual area. A 24 px icon with 10 px of transparent padding is a 44 px target that still looks like a 24 px icon.
symptoms: users keep mis-tapping|delete sits right next to save|it is fiddly on mobile|the submit button is miles from the last field
quote: The time to acquire a target is a function of the distance to and size of the target. - lawsofux.com

name: Hick's Law
claim: Decision time rises with the entropy of the option set rather than the raw count, so the cost is logarithmic and cheap.
key_number: ~5 bits/s (Hick 1952); b ~ 200 ms/bit
formula: RT = a + b*log2(n+1); general RT = a + b*H where H = sum p*log2(1/p)
design_lever: Skew the probability distribution instead of deleting options: one visually dominant primary action, a marked recommended tier, relevance sorting, and the last choice remembered.
anti_pattern: Do not delete features to hit an item count and rebuild them as three levels of nesting. Net decision cost rises while the organisation congratulates itself on simplicity.
symptoms: too many options on this screen|users freeze at the plan picker|the menu is too long|should we nest these under a submenu
quote: Be careful not to simplify to the point of abstraction. - lawsofux.com

name: Doherty Threshold
claim: Productivity rises superlinearly when system response stays under 400 ms, because the user never drops out of the interaction loop.
key_number: 400ms (Doherty & Thadani 1982); 0.1s/1s/10s (R. B. Miller 1968); 16 ms for direct manipulation
design_lever: Acknowledge every press locally within 100 ms without waiting on a round trip, then set p95 budgets per interaction class and treat a breach as a bug with a named owner.
anti_pattern: Do not stage a fake progress sequence over work that did not happen. An artificial delay that depicts real work is honest pacing; one that fabricates work is a lie about the product.
symptoms: the app feels sluggish|users click twice|nothing happens when I press it|the spinner flickers on fast operations
quote: Productivity soars when a computer and its users interact at a pace (<400ms) that ensures that neither has to wait on the other. - lawsofux.com

name: Jakob's Law
claim: Users spend most of their time on other products and therefore expect yours to work the same way as those.
key_number: none; power law of learning
design_lever: Conform on interaction mechanics - select, scroll, undo, back, submit - and spend your differentiation budget on capability and visual identity instead.
anti_pattern: Do not ship a near-miss. A control that is 90% conventional causes negative transfer and is measurably slower and more error-prone than either full conformity or overt novelty.
symptoms: users cannot find the cart|the custom dropdown confuses people|everyone hates the redesign|our terminology is clever and nobody understands it
quote: Users prefer your site to work the same way as all the other sites they already know. - Jakob Nielsen

name: Postel's Law
claim: Be liberal in the syntax you accept from a human and strict about the semantics you require from them.
design_lever: Run all four steps in order: accept variable input, translate it to your requirements, define the boundary, then echo the parsed result back so a misreading is visible.
anti_pattern: Do not carry liberal acceptance past the presentation layer. Fuzzy-matching a login identifier, or accepting anything into the trust boundary, is a security hole dressed as kindness.
symptoms: the form rejects my phone number|why can I not paste my card number|validation only fails on submit|it will not take a space in the postcode
quote: Be liberal in what you accept, and conservative in what you send. - lawsofux.com

name: Tesler's Law
claim: Every process has a core of complexity that cannot be removed, only allocated between the system and the user.
key_number: engineer-week ~40 h vs user-minute x 100k users ~1,667 h
design_lever: For every proposed simplification, name who now does the work and whether you can see them doing it. If the answer is support or the customer's ops team, the simplification is fake.
anti_pattern: Do not strip an interface to three buttons and call it simple when the removed capability became contact support. C_user went up and only the screenshot improved.
symptoms: we simplified it and support tickets went up|the new version cannot do what I need|it looks clean but I cannot finish the task|users email us to change it now
quote: All processes have a core of complexity that cannot be designed away and therefore must be assumed by either the system or the user. - lawsofux.com

name: Law of Pragnanz
claim: When a visual field admits several readings, perception collapses pre-consciously to the one with fewest parts and most regularity.
key_number: none
design_lever: Blur the mock to 8 px, count the units you see and where the boundaries fall, then compare that list against the information architecture you intended.
anti_pattern: Do not use it as an argument for removing labels. Pragnanz finds a simplest reading, not the correct one, and bare glyphs get confidently read as the wrong affordance.
symptoms: is this a button|the icon-only toolbar confuses people|the layout reads wrong at a glance|users cannot tell what is clickable
quote: People will perceive and interpret ambiguous or complex images as the simplest form possible. - lawsofux.com

name: Law of Proximity
claim: Elements group when the gap between them is smaller than the gap to everything else; grouping reads the ratio, not the absolute distance.
key_number: between-group gap / within-group gap >= 2 (marginal at 1.5)
design_lever: Make the between-group gap at least twice the within-group gap - 8 px inside a field group, 24 px between groups - before you reach for a border.
anti_pattern: Do not set a label 12 px above its input and 12 px below the previous input. Every label becomes ambiguous and users answer the wrong question.
symptoms: users answer the wrong field|the caption looks like it belongs to the next image|everything runs together|the spacing is uniform everywhere
quote: Objects that are near, or proximate to each other, tend to be grouped together. - lawsofux.com

name: Law of Similarity
claim: Elements sharing a visual attribute are perceived as related and as sharing function, even when they are far apart.
key_number: none; WCAG 1.4.1 forbids colour as the only channel
design_lever: Enforce the invariant in both directions: same appearance means same behaviour, and different behaviour means different appearance. Exactly one primary button style per view.
anti_pattern: Do not style a destructive action with the secondary-button token. Similarity is the only grouping cue that can assert something false, and design systems enforce only half the invariant.
symptoms: two primary buttons on one screen|users click the wrong action|status colours mean different things on different pages|the disabled state looks like body text
quote: Ensure that links and navigation systems are visually differentiated from normal text elements. - lawsofux.com

name: Law of Common Region
claim: Elements inside a bounded area group together, and this beats proximity and similarity when the cues are put in conflict.
key_number: Palmer 1992; background tint ~3-5% luminance delta suffices; ~2 nesting levels maximum
design_lever: Escalate grouping strength in order - gap, background tint, border, elevation - and only when the previous rung visibly fails a squint test.
anti_pattern: Do not draw a card you cannot name. A region is a semantic claim, so if you cannot say which entity it represents it should have been spacing instead.
symptoms: the page is card soup|too many boxes|the grouping disappears in dark mode|nested cards with no hierarchy
quote: Elements tend to be perceived into groups if they are sharing an area with a clearly defined boundary. - lawsofux.com

name: Law of Uniform Connectedness
claim: Visibly connected elements read as more related than unconnected ones: a connector defeats a gap and a gap never defeats a connector.
key_number: Palmer & Rock 1994; connectors below ~3:1 contrast stop working
design_lever: Spend connectors only on relations that carry more than membership - sequence, hierarchy, dependency, shared state - and express membership with spacing or a region.
anti_pattern: Do not float a tab bar with a gap beneath it. The merged edge between active tab and panel is the cue that the panel belongs to that tab, and without it the panel is misread.
symptoms: the stepper does not read as steps|users do not connect the tab to its content|the table has lines everywhere|the flow diagram arrows mean nothing
quote: Elements that are visually connected are perceived as more related than elements with no connection. - lawsofux.com

name: Aesthetic-Usability Effect
claim: Attractive interfaces are rated as more usable and forgiven minor problems, chiefly on first impression rather than in daily use.
key_number: Kurosu & Kashimura 1995: 26 ATM variants, 252 participants; Tuch 2012, n=80, found no effect
design_lever: Weight behavioural metrics above self-report, log them separately rather than blending them, and hold visual fidelity constant across any two arms you compare.
anti_pattern: Do not accept a satisfaction score from a polished prototype as usability evidence. A large gap between no problems reported and task failed is the signature of this effect, not noise.
symptoms: it tested well but the funnel is bad|users said they liked it and still could not finish|which of these two mocks should we ship|the exec approved it from a screenshot
quote: Visually pleasing design can mask usability problems and prevent issues from being discovered during usability testing. - lawsofux.com

name: Goal-Gradient Effect
claim: Effort accelerates as perceived remaining distance to a goal shrinks, so abandonment is front-loaded rather than concentrated at the end.
key_number: 19% to 34% completion (Nunes & Dreze 2006, n~300, 9 months)
design_lever: Show fractional progress, pre-tick the steps the user genuinely already completed, and measure abandonment per step rather than in aggregate.
anti_pattern: Never let the denominator change after the flow starts. A counter whose total grows mid-flow inverts the effect into betrayal at the exact moment the user notices.
symptoms: nobody finishes onboarding|users drop out of the signup form|the checkout has too many steps|activation stalls early
quote: The tendency to approach a goal increases with proximity to the goal. - lawsofux.com

name: Zeigarnik Effect
claim: Interrupted tasks are remembered better than completed ones. The pooled recall advantage across the literature is approximately zero.
key_number: pooled interrupted:completed recall ~ 0.99 (Ghibellini & Meier 2025); Ovsiankina resumption ~ two-thirds
design_lever: Cite resumption rather than recall: build saved drafts, abandoned-cart re-entry and resume-where-you-left-off, and give every loop you open a reachable close.
anti_pattern: Do not build an uncleanable badge or an endless feed and call it Zeigarnik. The recall claim is null, and a badge that never reaches zero destroys the signal value of every badge you ship.
symptoms: users never come back to finish|the unread count never clears|people abandon halfway and never return|should we add a red dot
quote: People remember uncompleted or interrupted tasks better than completed tasks. - lawsofux.com

name: Peak-End Rule
claim: An episode is judged by its most intense moment and its final moment rather than by its sum or its duration.
key_number: colonoscopy RCT n=682; cold pressor 60 s at 14 C vs 60 s + 30 s at 15 C; end window ~ last 3 min
design_lever: Find and remove the worst moment first using error-rate and support-ticket data, then design the terminal screen of each bounded task rather than of the product.
anti_pattern: Do not fire confetti over a flow that just lost the user's data. Negativity bias makes the peak negative in most software, and a celebration on top of it reads as mockery.
symptoms: users remember the one time it broke|the confirmation screen is an afterthought|churned customers warn other people|the cancellation flow is hostile
quote: People judge an experience largely based on how they felt at its peak and at its end, rather than the total sum or average of every moment. - lawsofux.com

name: Von Restorff Effect
claim: In a homogeneous set the item that differs is found and remembered best, so salience is a zero-sum budget.
key_number: distinctiveness ~ (n-k)/n per emphasised item
design_lever: Budget one pre-attentive isolate per viewport and at most one secondary, and verify each survives greyscale rendering and prefers-reduced-motion.
anti_pattern: Do not let every stakeholder win their component a highlight. When twelve items among twelve are emphasised, nothing is emphasised and the page is merely loud.
symptoms: users do not see the primary action|everything on the page shouts|which plan should we highlight|the status dots are colour only
quote: Use restraint when placing emphasis on visual elements to avoid them competing with one another. - lawsofux.com

name: Flow
claim: Absorption requires perceived challenge and perceived skill to be matched and both above that individual's own average.
key_number: latency budget 400 ms (Doherty), ~100 ms per interaction
formula: C/S ~ 1 AND C > C_mean, S > S_mean
design_lever: Treat it as a list of things not to do: no interruption during an active task, no unfed wait over 400 ms, no forced mode switch, no difficulty fixed at design time.
anti_pattern: Do not conflate flow with ease. Matched challenge and skill at low levels produces apathy, and a goal of make everything effortless targets relaxation instead.
symptoms: power users say the tool gets in the way|the modal interrupts my work|experts find it tedious and novices find it terrifying|I lose my place every time it saves
quote: The mental state in which a person performing some activity is fully immersed in a feeling of energized focus, full involvement, and enjoyment. - lawsofux.com

name: Parkinson's Law
claim: A task expands to fill the time allowed, and satisfaction tracks the gap between expected and actual duration.
key_number: bureaucracy growth 5-7% per year (Parkinson 1955)
design_lever: Give the task the smallest honest container you can and beat it: cut fields, set every autocomplete attribute, state the true duration, finish under it.
anti_pattern: Do not read this as impose time pressure. A countdown that resets on reload compresses deliberation with a false claim and is actionable in several jurisdictions.
symptoms: the form takes too long|users abandon at the address step|should we add a countdown to the offer|we say two minutes and it takes fifteen
quote: Any task will inflate until all of the available time is spent. - lawsofux.com

name: Choice Overload
claim: A large assortment suppresses choice and satisfaction only when the options must be evaluated rather than merely recognised.
key_number: 30% vs 3% purchase at 6 vs 24 jams (Iyengar & Lepper 2000); meta-analytic mean ~ 0 (Scheibehenne 2010, N=5036)
design_lever: Run the four-part check before cutting anything - set complexity, task difficulty, preference uncertainty, decision goal - and name which moderator is active here.
anti_pattern: Do not delete a capability because users seem overwhelmed. The evidence supports staging the set, not shrinking it, and the effect vanishes for a returning user who knows what they want.
symptoms: too many plans to choose from|users bounce off the catalogue|the settings page is overwhelming|should we cut the product range
quote: The tendency for people to get overwhelmed when they are presented with a large number of options. - lawsofux.com

name: Occam's Razor
claim: Among designs that serve the task equally well, the one with the fewest parts should be selected.
key_number: none
design_lever: Ask of each element: what breaks if this is gone? If nobody can name a user-visible consequence, remove it. That turns an aesthetic into a testable claim per element.
anti_pattern: Do not drop the clause that predict equally well. Stripping labels off icons, or hiding desktop navigation behind a hamburger, trades visible complexity for hidden search cost.
symptoms: this screen has too much on it|can we remove this field|the design feels cluttered|do we need this setting
quote: Among competing hypotheses that predict equally well, the one with the fewest assumptions should be selected. - lawsofux.com

name: Pareto Principle
claim: Impact is skewed, so a small share of inputs produces most of the outcome. The exact ratio is a free parameter, not a constant.
key_number: 80/20 corresponds to alpha = log4(5) ~ 1.161; NN/g report 5% of pages carrying 67% of pageviews
design_lever: Build the cumulative distribution from your own telemetry, cut the roadmap where the curve flattens, and state explicitly that everything below the line is deferred, not deleted.
anti_pattern: Do not treat the tail as trivial. Juran renamed it the useful many for exactly this reason, and only 2% of users need this is the most common accessibility failure in product work.
symptoms: which features should get top-level placement|we cannot fix everything|what should we optimise first|nobody uses that feature
quote: The Pareto principle states that, for many events, roughly 80% of the effects come from 20% of the causes. - lawsofux.com

name: Mental Model
claim: Users interact with an internal simulation built from other products; when the system disagrees, they experience the system as broken.
key_number: none
formula: designer model -> system image -> user model
design_lever: Ask what a stranger would infer from this screen alone. The system image is your only channel, so a model you can convey only by explaining has not been conveyed.
anti_pattern: Do not mirror the database schema in the navigation. The team already knows the data model, and users are then asked to learn the org chart to find a setting.
symptoms: users expect back to go back|nobody understands our terminology|the navigation matches our teams not their tasks|two search bars confuse people
quote: A compressed model based on what we think we know about a system and how it works. - lawsofux.com

name: Cognitive Bias
claim: Human judgement deviates from rational choice in predictable, repeatable directions, so the deviations can be measured and designed around.
key_number: ~180 catalogued biases; Tversky & Kahneman 1974 named three heuristics
design_lever: For every persuasive mechanism in the design, ask whether it would still work if a caption on the same screen explained it. If disclosure kills it, it was running on deception.
anti_pattern: Do not use cognitive bias as a post-hoc explanation for a result. With roughly 180 catalogued biases one can be found to rationalise any outcome, which is unfalsifiable and worthless.
symptoms: is this a dark pattern|users feel tricked|the pre-ticked box keeps converting|the team explains away every usability finding
quote: A systematic error of thinking or rationality in judgment that influence our perception of the world. - lawsofux.com

name: Paradox of the Active User
claim: Users do not read documentation; they start immediately and absorb errors, because reading has poor expected value across most software.
key_number: none; observational (Carroll & Rosson 1987), no effect size published
design_lever: Move instruction into empty states, field hints, first-use affordances and error text, and lower the cost of a wrong guess with undo, autosave and non-destructive defaults.
anti_pattern: Do not apply this to high-consequence, low-frequency expert domains such as clinical dosing, aviation or tax filing. There exploration is unacceptable and nobody reads is a safety failure.
symptoms: users skip the onboarding tour|nobody reads the help article|they call support instead of reading the tooltip|the coach marks get clicked through
quote: Users never read manuals but start using the software immediately. - lawsofux.com

name: Endowed Progress Effect
claim: Re-expressing progress the user already made as a head start raises completion, at identical real required effort.
key_number: 19% (8-stamp) vs 34% (10-stamp with 2 pre-applied), n~300 over 9 months (Nunes & Dreze 2006)
design_lever: Start every checklist and completeness meter non-empty by crediting what the user genuinely already did - account created, email verified - before they first see it.
anti_pattern: Do not inflate the denominator. Adding two free steps to a requirement that was eight steps long is fiction, and the tell is whether you would show the user both versions side by side.
symptoms: the setup checklist starts at zero|users do not begin the profile|activation stalls at step one|the progress bar feels discouraging

name: Social Proof
claim: People adapt their behaviour to what others do. The effect is reliable at scale and small in magnitude.
key_number: OPOWER energy reports: ATE 1.4-3.3%, unweighted mean ~2% across millions of households (Allcott 2011)
design_lever: Make the proof diagnostic - a review from someone with the same use case, a count drawn from the user's own segment - and test specific against generic rather than proof against none.
anti_pattern: Do not render a count with no data source, and never use negative proof. Only 12% of users complete this normalises the very behaviour you were trying to reduce.
symptoms: should we show how many people bought this|reviews are not converting|the testimonials feel fake|conversion is up but refunds are up too

name: Scarcity
claim: Perceived limited availability raises perceived value, and a transition from abundant to scarce beats constant scarcity.
key_number: Worchel, Lee & Adewole 1975: 200 undergraduates, lab only, single population
design_lever: Query the count from live inventory at render time and render nothing when the honest number is unimpressive. Show the change in availability rather than a permanent low-stock badge.
anti_pattern: Do not ship a timer that survives a page reload. Manufactured scarcity wins the A/B test and loses the cohort, and fabricated urgency is actionable under the EU and UK regimes.
symptoms: should we add only 2 left|the urgency banner is always on|conversion is up but trust scores fell|users stopped believing our stock counts

name: Framing
claim: Logically equivalent descriptions of the same outcome produce different preferences, and no presentation is unframed.
key_number: Tversky & Kahneman 1981, the Asian-disease problem
design_lever: Choose the frame that leaves users best informed, and append one comprehension question to the A/B test so understanding is measured alongside choice share.
anti_pattern: Do not defend a winning frame with we did not intend to influence them. You chose a frame either way, and a frame that wins because users misunderstand the offer is deception.
symptoms: how should we word the pricing|users misunderstand what they signed up for|the copy converts but people complain later|monthly or annual framing

name: Availability
claim: People judge frequency and risk by how easily instances come to mind, so whatever is on screen becomes their evidence base.
key_number: Tversky & Kahneman 1973
design_lever: Treat every omission from a comparison as a thumb on the scale, and list the attribute you lose on rather than leaving the user unable to weigh it at all.
anti_pattern: Do not make a rare risk vivid in order to sell relief from it. Proportionality to the actual base rate is the line between safety communication and exploitation.
symptoms: users overreact to the one outage|the comparison table hides our weak spot|people think this is riskier than it is|the roadmap follows the loudest recent incident

name: Representativeness
claim: Probability is judged by resemblance to a prototype and ignores base rates, producing stereotyping and base-rate neglect.
key_number: Kahneman & Tversky 1972; the Linda conjunction problem 1983
design_lever: Surface the base rate wherever the interface asks somebody to judge likelihood: show the actual approval rate beside the application form, the real incidence beside the symptom.
anti_pattern: Do not use this one to persuade. Every application to a person is stereotyping with a technical name, and encoding it in a risk model industrialises the bias behind a veneer of objectivity.
symptoms: the fraud rule flags the wrong people|our screening narrows the pool|users judge by appearance|the model is confident and wrong on one segment

name: Anchoring
claim: An initial number shifts subsequent judgements, and it keeps working even when the anchor is known to be arbitrary.
key_number: 3.3 to 7.0 cans under a limit-12 sign (Wansink, Kent & Hoch 1998 - cite with the Wansink misconduct context attached)
design_lever: Anchor on real reference points - an actual former price, a real competitor price, the median order for comparable customers - and audit every anchor as a factual claim.
anti_pattern: Do not invent a limit or a was-price. A Limit 12 sign is read as information about supply, so if no supply constraint exists you have made a false statement in a font.
symptoms: which price should be listed first|the middle tier is not converting|should we show a struck-through price|users anchor on the cheapest plan

name: Priming
claim: Exposure to a cue makes related concepts more accessible. Lexical priming replicates; social and behavioural priming did not.
key_number: Meyer & Schvaneveldt 1971 holds; Doyen et al. 2012 found nothing for behavioural priming
design_lever: Use lexical priming freely - autocomplete, query suggestions, priming the right conceptual frame before a complex explanation - and expect small effects.
anti_pattern: Do not build on behavioural priming. Kahneman conceded in 2017 that he had placed too much faith in underpowered studies on exactly this material, so a large reported lift is an underpowered test.
symptoms: do trust badges before the payment field help|will this microcopy change behaviour|the security icons tested well on a small sample|can we prime users to feel safe

name: Sunk Cost Fallacy and Loss Aversion
claim: Irrecoverable past investment improperly sways forward choices. Losses may loom larger than gains, but the 2x constant does not hold generally.
key_number: 85% continued a doomed project vs 10% investing fresh (Arkes & Blumer 1985); lambda ~ 2.25 contested (Gal & Rucker 2018)
design_lever: Apply the exportability test: if the user can take the accumulated value with them and the product still holds them, the value was real rather than engineered regret.
anti_pattern: Do not inventory what a departing user will lose. A streak with no learning value exists only to be lost, and selling a freeze for it monetises anxiety you manufactured.
symptoms: users stay but never use it|should we add streaks|the cancellation flow lists everything they lose|churn is low and engagement is dead

name: CAR Model (Cue-Action-Reward)
claim: A cue followed promptly by a reward strengthens the action until it runs automatically, and variable schedules resist extinction most.
key_number: variable-ratio schedules give maximum resistance to extinction (Ferster & Skinner 1957)
design_lever: Build the loop around an action the user would endorse in a calm moment, and measure cue-to-action latency, which shortens as automaticity develops.
anti_pattern: Do not reach for a variable reward schedule without asking why a fixed one is insufficient. If the honest answer is because users would stop, you have designed a compulsion.
symptoms: how do we make this a habit|engagement drops after week two|should notifications be unpredictable|users forget to come back

name: Reward Learning
claim: Contingent, prompt reinforcement raises behaviour frequency, but extrinsic reward can reduce intrinsic motivation for an already-valued activity.
key_number: overjustification effect (Deci 1971; Deci, Koestner & Ryan 1999 meta-analysis)
design_lever: Reinforce behaviours that are effortful and unrewarding in themselves - expense reports, form completion, flossing - and run the removal test with a holdout after a month.
anti_pattern: Do not reinforce a behaviour the user already enjoys. Remove the points later and behaviour drops below where it started, which is worse than never having added them.
symptoms: should we add points and badges|engagement spiked then collapsed|users only do it for the reward|the streak matters more than the task

name: Optimal Challenge
claim: Difficulty must track rising skill, so a system with static difficulty falls out of the challenge-skill band by default.
key_number: productive success band roughly 60-85% per attempt - calibrate for your domain, do not assume
design_lever: Ship a novice surface and an expert surface in the same product - command palette, bulk actions, raw query mode - so challenge can rise as the user's skill does.
anti_pattern: Do not inflate difficulty to sell relief from it. That turns challenge tuning into manufactured frustration with a purchasable exit, which is a scarcity play in a difficulty costume.
symptoms: experts find it tedious|new users are terrified|the tool is either too basic or too hard|power users have outgrown the UI

name: Cognitive Load Balancing
claim: Presenting information in small progressive fragments raises task performance, because only the extraneous share of load is reducible.
key_number: NASA-TLX for subjective load; help-seeking per step as the field proxy
design_lever: Map searches, doc opens and support contacts per step across the whole flow. The spike points straight at the screen carrying the extraneous load.
anti_pattern: Do not strip germane load along with extraneous. An interface so frictionless that users build no mental model leaves them helpless the first time anything deviates.
symptoms: users need training to use this|easy to start and impossible to master|too many concepts at once|the onboarding tour covers everything

name: Stimulus Devaluation
claim: Inserting delay or friction between an action and its reward weakens the cue-action association that makes the behaviour automatic.
key_number: none; extrapolated from outcome-devaluation work (Adams & Dickinson 1981), which diagnoses habit rather than preventing it
design_lever: State the inverted success metrics before you build: cue-to-action latency should lengthen and session frequency should fall, and say so to whoever owns the engagement dashboard.
anti_pattern: Do not point this at a habit the user wants. Friction added to cancelling, exporting or switching is the same mechanism turned against the person it was meant to protect.
symptoms: users say they open it compulsively|we want to reduce doomscrolling|the app is too sticky for its own good|people regret the time they spend here

name: Stopping Rules
claim: People consume until a stopping cue arrives, so removing the cue lets fatigue rather than intention govern how much they consume.
key_number: none; Simon satisficing plus the consumption-cue literature
design_lever: Give every consumption surface a designed endpoint even if reaching it is optional: an end-of-feed marker, a caught-up state, a session summary, an episode limit.
anti_pattern: Do not remove the endpoint and call it engagement. The harm is the absence of something, which makes it invisible in design review and unattributable in a changelog.
symptoms: sessions run longer than users intend|the feed never ends|autoplay keeps rolling|users cannot tell when they are done

name: Choice Architecture
claim: The arrangement of options changes what people choose, and since no arrangement is neutral the default is the design decision.
key_number: opt-out organ-donation consent above 90% vs low teens for opt-in (Johnson & Goldstein 2003)
design_lever: Write the default-setting rationale down at review beside the counterfactual - what would the user have chosen with full attention - and prefer the weaker, more visible lever when unsure.
anti_pattern: Do not launder a revenue decision with there is no neutral default. If opting out is materially harder than opting in that is sludge, and the click-count ratio is the evidence.
symptoms: what should this toggle default to|the consent banner has one big accept button|users do not know what they agreed to|nobody changes the setting

name: Ambient Communication
claim: State encoded in pre-attentive attributes can be read at a glance, at negligible attentional cost compared with text or numerals.
key_number: none; Weiser & Brown 1996, calm technology
design_lever: Encode state in colour, size, orientation or closure and test with brief exposure: flash the display for a fixed short interval and score accuracy of state recall against the numeric equivalent.
anti_pattern: Do not let an ambient display become a nag. A ring that shows state is calm; a ring that shows an unmet daily obligation is a recurring low-grade demand.
symptoms: the dashboard needs to be readable at a glance|users miss the build status|the badge is permanently red|too many numbers to scan

name: Optimal Information Flow
claim: The same information in a different order produces a different load, because load depends on what must be held simultaneously.
key_number: none; Baymard checkout research attributes much cart abandonment to flow rather than price
design_lever: Before deleting a field, reorder so each step is answerable with what the user knows at that moment, and use field-level abandonment to locate where the order broke.
anti_pattern: Do not make the exit path longer than the entry path. If cancellation has more steps than signup, that asymmetry needs a justification that is not retention.
symptoms: users abandon at one specific field|the checkout asks for things too early|the signup order feels wrong|people back up to fix an earlier answer

name: Personalisation
claim: A recommender trained on revealed preference amplifies whatever it observes, and its effect compounds as data accumulates.
key_number: none; offline metrics such as precision@k and NDCG measure agreement with historical behaviour
design_lever: Run a random or popularity-ranked holdout so you learn what share of engagement the model actually produces, and expose the main inferences for the user to correct.
anti_pattern: Do not pick engagement as the objective because it was the metric already available. The objective function is the most consequential decision in a personalised product and it is usually made by default.
symptoms: recommendations feel narrow|users cannot change what they are shown|engagement is up but retention is flat|the empty state never improves

name: Gamification
claim: Game elements raise engagement, but the behavioural effect is the smallest and least stable of the measured outcomes.
key_number: cognitive g=0.49, motivational g=0.36, behavioural g=0.25 (Sailer & Homner 2020)
design_lever: Disaggregate before adopting: name which of progress, feedback, social comparison and loss aversion is doing the work, and check each would survive on its own.
anti_pattern: Do not measure engagement with the game layer instead of progress on the real goal. Badges for logging in certify nothing, and the removal test tells you whether you built motivation or dependence.
symptoms: should we gamify this|the leaderboard demotivates half the team|users chase points instead of the outcome|badges are not moving the real metric
